key_concepts_expected: Financial statements are formal financial reports that show the financial performance
and financial position of a company for a particular period.
They are mainly prepared to understand:
questions.source_answer_text:
Financial statements are formal financial reports that show the financial performance
and financial position of a company for a particular period.
They are mainly prepared to understand:
• How much revenue and profit the company generated.
• What assets and liabilities the company has.
• How much cash the company generated and used.
• The overall financial health of the business.
Financial statements are also used by management, investors, lenders, analysts, and
other stakeholders to make financial and business decisions.
The three main financial statements are the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and
Cash Flow Statement.

questions.text: How are the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement interconnected?
key_concepts_expected: The three financial statements are closely interconnected.
The Net Income from the Income Statement flows into Retained Earnings in the
Balance Sheet.
questions.source_answer_text:
The three financial statements are closely interconnected.
The Net Income from the Income Statement  flows into Retained Earnings in the
Balance Sheet.
Net Income also becomes the starting point of the Operating Activities section of the
Cash Flow Statement under the indirect method.
The Cash Flow Statement explains the change in cash between the beginning and ending
periods. The ending cash balance from the Cash Flow Statement appears as Cash and
Cash Equivalents on the Balance Sheet.
Changes in Balance Sheet items such as:
• Accounts Receivable
• Inventory
• Accounts Payable
• Debt
• Fixed Assets
affect the Cash Flow Statement.
For example, if Accounts Receivable increases, revenue may have been recognized but
cash has not yet been collected. Therefore, it reduces operating cash flow.
So, in simple terms:
Income Statement → Profit/Loss
Balance Sheet → Assets, Liabilities & Equity
Cash Flow Statement → Movement of Cash
All three statements should be linked in a properly built financial model.

questions.text: What is depreciation? Explain its methods with an example.
key_concepts_expected: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its
useful life.
It is a non-cash expense, meaning the company does not make a cash payment every
questions.source_answer_text:
Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its
useful life.
It is a non-cash expense, meaning the company does not make a cash payment every
year for depreciation. The cash outflow generally occurs when the asset is purchased.
Common depreciation methods include:
Straight-Line Method:
Under this method, the same amount of depreciation is charged every year.
Formula:
Depreciation = (Cost of Asset − Salvage Value) / Useful Life
Example:
Asset cost = ₹10 crore
Salvage value = ₹1 crore
Useful life = 9 years
Depreciation:
(₹10 crore − ₹1 crore) / 9 = ₹1 crore per year
Written Down Value / Declining Balance Method:
Under this method, depreciation is calculated on the asset's carrying value. Therefore,
depreciation is generally higher in the earlier years and decreases over time.
The method used depends on the applicable accounting framework and the nature of the
asset.

questions.text: What is the difference between CapEx, OpEx and COGS? How does CapEx affect the Financial Statements?
key_concepts_expected: CapEx — Capital Expenditure
CapEx is spending on assets that provide benefits over multiple periods.
Examples:
questions.source_answer_text:
CapEx — Capital Expenditure
CapEx is spending on assets that provide benefits over multiple periods.  Examples:
• Purchase of machinery
• Purchase of buildings
• Purchase of equipment
• Major investments in long-term assets
CapEx is generally capitalized on the Balance Sheet rather than immediately expensed.
OpEx — Operating Expenditure
OpEx represents expenses incurred to run the normal operations of the business.
Examples:
• Salaries
• Rent
• Advertising
• Office expenses
• Utilities
OpEx is generally recorded as an expense in the Income Statement in the period in which
it is incurred.
COGS — Cost of Goods Sold
COGS represents the direct costs associated with producing or purchasing the goods
that are sold.
Examples:
• Raw materials
• Direct production labor
• Manufacturing costs directly related to production
COGS is deducted from revenue to calculate Gross Profit.
Impact of CapEx on Financial Statements:
Suppose a company purchases machinery for ₹10 crore using cash.
Income Statement:
There is generally no immediate ₹10 crore expense. Instead, depreciation is recognized
over the asset's useful life.  Balance Sheet:
PPE increases by ₹10 crore and cash decreases by ₹10 crore.
Cash Flow Statement:
₹10 crore is shown as an outflow under Investing Activities.

EBITDA means Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization.
The relationship is:
questions.source_answer_text:
EBIT means Earnings Before Interest and Taxes.
EBITDA means Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization.
The relationship is:
EBITDA = EBIT + Depreciation + Amortization
For example:

EBITDA:

EBITDA is often used to compare operating performance before depreciation and
amortization, while EBIT includes the impact of these expenses.

questions.text: What is EPS? Explain the types of EPS with formula.
key_concepts_expected: EPS stands for Earnings Per Share .
It shows the amount of profit attributable to each
outstanding common equity share.
questions.source_answer_text:
EPS stands for Earnings Per Share . It shows the amount of profit attributable to each
outstanding common equity share.
The basic formula is:
Basic EPS = (Net Income − Preference Dividends) / Weighted Average Number of
Ordinary Shares Outstanding
For example:
Net Income = ₹100 crore
Preference Dividend = ₹10 crore
Weighted Average Shares = 18 crore  Basic EPS:
₹90 crore / 18 crore = ₹5 per share
There are two commonly discussed types:
Basic EPS:
Calculated using the actual weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding.
Diluted EPS:
Considers potential ordinary shares that could reduce EPS, such as:
• Stock options
• Convertible bonds
• Convertible preference shares
Formula: Diluted EPS = Adjusted Earnings / Adjusted Weighted Average Shares
Diluted EPS is generally equal to or lower than Basic EPS, except in certain anti -dilutive
situations where potential shares are excluded.

questions.text: Explain any Balance Sheet line item such as Treasury Stock, Retained Earnings, Deferred Revenue and Non-Controlling Interest.
key_concepts_expected: Treasury Stock:
Treasury stock represents a company's own shares that it has repurchased from the
market and has not retired.
questions.source_answer_text:
Treasury Stock:
Treasury stock represents a company's own shares that it has repurchased from the
market and has not retired.
It is generally shown as a deduction from shareholders' equity.
Example:
If a company spends ₹5 crore to repurchase its own shares, cash decreases by ₹5 crore
and shareholders' equity also decreases by ₹5 crore.
Retained Earnings:
Retained earnings represent the accumulated profits of the company that have not been
distributed to shareholders as dividends.
Basic relationship:
Closing Retained Earnings = Opening Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends  Deferred Revenue / Contract Liability:
Deferred revenue occurs when a company receives cash from a customer before it has
delivered the related goods or services.
For example, if a customer pays ₹12 lakh in advance for a one-year service contract, the
company does not immediately recognize the entire ₹12 lakh as revenue. The amount is
initially recorded as a liability and recognized as revenue as the service is provided.
Non-Controlling Interest (NCI):
NCI represents the portion of a subsidiary's equity that is owned by shareholders other
than the parent company.
For example, if a parent company owns 80% of a subsidiary, the remaining 20%
represents the non-controlling interest.

questions.text: A company's revenue increased by 20%, but its cash balance decreased significantly. What would you investigate?
key_concepts_expected: I would not assume that higher revenue automatically means higher cash.
I would
investigate the Cash Flow Statement and Balance Sheet to understand where the cash
questions.source_answer_text:
I would not assume that higher revenue automatically means higher cash. I would
investigate the Cash Flow Statement and Balance Sheet to understand where the cash
was used.
First, I would check Accounts Receivable. If revenue increased because of credit sales
but customers have not yet paid, Accounts Receivable may have increased significantly.
Second, I would check Inventory. The company may have invested heavily in inventory
in preparation for future sales.
Third, I would check Capital Expenditure. The company may have purchased machinery,
buildings, or other fixed assets.
Fourth, I would check Debt repayment, dividends, or share buybacks , which are
financing cash outflows.
I would also investigate whether operating expenses, interest payments, or taxes
increased significantly.
Therefore, I would analyze the Cash Flow Statement, working capital movements,
Balance Sheet changes, and financing activities  to identify the reason for the decline
in cash.

questions.text: A company reports ₹50 crore of net profit but has negative cash flow from operations. What could be the reasons?
key_concepts_expected: Net profit and operating cash flow are different because profit is calculated using accrual
accounting, while cash flow measures actual cash movement.
Possible reasons include:
questions.source_answer_text:
Net profit and operating cash flow are different because profit is calculated using accrual
accounting, while cash flow measures actual cash movement.
Possible reasons include:
Increase in Accounts Receivable:
The company may have recognized significant sales but has not collected the cash from
customers.
Increase in Inventory:
The company may have purchased large amounts of inventory, resulting in cash outflow.
Decrease in Accounts Payable:
The company may have paid suppliers faster, causing cash to decrease.
Other working capital changes:
Prepaid expenses or other current assets may have increased.
Large non-cash or accrual-related adjustments:
The reported profit may include items that do not represent current-period operating
cash receipts.
Therefore, I would reconcile Net Income to Operating Cash Flow and examine changes in
Accounts Receivable, Inventory, Accounts Payable, and other working capital items.

questions.text: What is Ratio Analysis?
key_concepts_expected: Ratio analysis is a financial analysis technique used to evaluate the performance,
financial position, and efficiency of a company by comparing different figures from its
financial statements.
questions.source_answer_text:
Ratio analysis is a financial analysis technique used to evaluate the performance,
financial position, and efficiency of a company by comparing different figures from its
financial statements.
Ratios generally compare two related financial figures, such as profit to sales, current
assets to current liabilities, or debt to equity.
For example:
Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
If a company has current assets of ₹10 lakh and current liabilities of ₹5 lakh:
Current Ratio = ₹10 lakh ÷ ₹5 lakh = 2.0x
This means the company has ₹2 of current assets for every ₹1 of current liabilities.
Ratio analysis helps management, investors, lenders, and analysts understand
profitability, liquidity, efficiency, solvency, and market performance.

questions.text: Why do companies perform Ratio Analysis?

Companies perform ratio analysis to understand their financial performance and identify

The major purposes are:
• Measure profitability:  To understand how efficiently the company generates
profits.
• Measure liquidity: To determine whether the company can meet its short -term
obligations.
• Measure efficiency: To evaluate how effectively the company uses its assets and
working capital.
• Measure solvency: To assess the company's ability to meet its long -term debt
obligations.
• Compare performance:  Ratios can be compared with previous years,
competitors, or industry benchmarks.
• Support decision-making: Management can use ratios for financial planning and
strategic decisions.
• Identify financial risks: Ratios can highlight increasing debt, declining margins,
slow collections, or inefficient inventory management.

key_concepts_expected: Profitability ratios measure the company's ability to generate profit from its sales, assets,

questions.source_answer_text:
Profitability ratios measure the company's ability to generate profit from its sales, assets,
equity, and invested capital.
Important profitability ratios include:
1. Gross Profit Margin
Gross Profit Margin = Gross Profit ÷ Revenue × 100
It measures how much profit remains after deducting the cost of goods sold.
2. Operating Profit Margin
Operating Profit Margin = EBIT ÷ Revenue × 100
It measures the profitability of the company's core operations.
3. Net Profit Margin
Net Profit Margin = Net Profit ÷ Revenue × 100
It shows how much net profit the company earns from every ₹1 of revenue.  4. Return on Assets (ROA)
ROA = Net Income ÷ Average Total Assets × 100
It measures how efficiently the company uses its assets to generate profit.
5. Return on Equity (ROE)
ROE = Net Income ÷ Average Shareholders' Equity × 100
It measures the return generated on shareholders' invested capital.
6. ROIC
ROIC = NOPAT ÷ Invested Capital × 100
It measures how efficiently the company generates operating returns from the capital
invested in the business.

questions.text: What is a Liquidity Ratio and what are its types?
key_concepts_expected: Liquidity ratios measure a company's ability to meet its short -term financial obligations
using its short-term assets.
The major liquidity ratios are:
questions.source_answer_text:
Liquidity ratios measure a company's ability to meet its short -term financial obligations
using its short-term assets.
The major liquidity ratios are:
1. Current Ratio
Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
It measures the company's overall short-term liquidity position.
2. Quick Ratio
Quick Ratio = Quick Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
Quick assets generally include cash, marketable securities, and accounts receivable.
Inventory is excluded because it may take time to convert into cash.
3. Cash Ratio
Cash Ratio = Cash and Cash Equivalents ÷ Current Liabilities
It is the most conservative liquidity ratio because it considers only cash and cash
equivalents against current liabilities.

questions.text: What is the difference between ROIC and ROCE?
key_concepts_expected: Both ROIC and ROCE measure returns generated from capital invested in the business,
but their definitions and formulas can vary between companies and analysts.
ROIC – Return on Invested Capital
questions.source_answer_text:
Both ROIC and ROCE measure returns generated from capital invested in the business,
but their definitions and formulas can vary between companies and analysts.
ROIC – Return on Invested Capital
A common formula is:  ROIC = NOPAT ÷ Invested Capital × 100
NOPAT means Net Operating Profit After Tax.
ROIC generally focuses on the after-tax operating return generated by capital invested in
the operating business.
ROCE – Return on Capital Employed
A common formula is:
ROCE = EBIT ÷ Capital Employed × 100
Capital employed is commonly calculated as:
Capital Employed = Total Assets − Current Liabilities
Therefore:
• ROIC generally uses NOPAT and invested capital.
• ROCE generally uses EBIT and capital employed.
• ROIC is often used to compare operating returns with the company's WACC.
• ROCE is commonly used to evaluate how efficiently long -term capital is being
employed.
Because definitions can vary, an analyst should always check how the company or data
provider calculates the ratio.

questions.text: What does a high Debt-to-Equity Ratio indicate?

Debt-to-Equity = Total Debt ÷ Shareholders' Equity

A high Debt-to-Equity ratio indicates that the company is using a relatively high amount
of debt compared with shareholders' equity.
Debt-to-Equity = Total Debt ÷ Shareholders' Equity
A higher ratio can indicate:
• Higher financial leverage
• Higher interest obligations
• Higher financial risk
• Greater sensitivity of profits to changes in interest rates and operating
performance
• Potentially higher ROE when the borrowed capital generates returns above its cost

stable cash flows and earns returns above the cost of debt, leverage can support growth
and shareholder returns.
The analyst should therefore examine debt maturity, interest rates, cash flows, and
interest coverage along with the debt-to-equity ratio.

• Inventory
• Accounts Payable

affect the Cash Flow Statement.

Balance Sheet → Assets, Liabilities & Equity
Cash Flow Statement → Movement of Cash

the operating business.

A common formula is:
ROCE = EBIT ÷ Capital Employed × 100

Capital Employed = Total Assets − Current Liabilities
Therefore:
• ROIC generally uses NOPAT and invested capital.
• ROCE generally uses EBIT and capital employed.
• ROIC is often used to compare operating returns with the company's WACC.
• ROCE is commonly used to evaluate how efficiently long -term capital is being
employed.
Because definitions can vary, an analyst should always check how the company or data
provider calculates the ratio.
